When solving an exercise inside [Chapter 15](../chapters/ch15-internal-pattern-matching-borders.qmd), [Chapter 16](../chapters/ch16-deterministic-tree-deque-pam.qmd), or [Chapter 17](../chapters/ch17-range-palindromes-rich-words.qmd), the surrounding section headings immediately tell you whether to deploy Kociumaka's Basic Substring Dictionary (`IPM`), an unamortized double-ended Palindromic Automaton (`Deque PAM`), or periodic suffix telescoping (`slink` cancellation). In a live contest, **substring and palindrome problems arrive with zero structural labels**. You are simply handed a string $S[1..N]$ and a stream of range queries $[l, r]$ or double-ended mutations, and you must diagnose which algebraic or combinatorial invariant governs the query.

This checkpoint tests **blind diagnostic recognition** across all three chapters of Part IV (`Ch 15`–`Ch 17`). None of the visible problem statements in Section 2 reveal which chapter or technique applies.

::: {.callout-important title="Zero-Spoiler Protocol & Progressive Hints"}

1. **Strict Zero-Spoiler Rule in Visible Statements**: Every problem statement (`CP-IV-01` through `CP-IV-07`) is written in pure contest form without naming the target chapter (`Ch 15`–`Ch 17`) or technique (`Bounded-Ratio IPM`, `Dyadic Border AP Intersection`, `quick_link / slink-Skip`, `Deque PAM Lazy Push-Down`, `Two-Boundary Range LPS Unclipping`, `slink Telescoping Cancellation`, `Factor-Closed Rich Words`).
2. **Diagnose Before Peeking**: Before opening any dropdown on a problem, write down on scratch paper:
   - Which **Part IV paradigm** (`Ch 15`–`Ch 17`) is triggered by the constraints and query geometry;
   - Which **lookalike decoy paradigm** must be ruled out, and why;
   - The **combinatorial word invariant** that collapses the naive $\Theta(N^2)$ or $\Theta(QN)$ bottleneck.
3. **Four-Stage Progressive Unmasking**:
   - **Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination**: Explains how to identify the governing paradigm and rule out lookalike decoys purely from constraints and query semantics.
   - **Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant**: States the exact periodicity, reflection, or telescoping identity needed for the reduction.
   - **Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly**: Outlines the state representation, preprocessing structures, and complexity target.
   - **Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution**: Full proof, boundary pitfall audit (`BP-4-01` through `BP-4-08`), and non-standard reference kernel where clarifying.

## 1. Blind Diagnostic Triage Guide & Decoy Elimination

The most dangerous traps in Part IV arise from **confusing two range-query or dynamic-window problems whose surface statements differ by a single word** (e.g., *"longest border of $S[l..r]$"* vs. *"longest palindrome of $S[l..r]$"*, or *"distinct palindromes in a sliding/deque window"* vs. *"distinct palindromes in an arbitrary range $S[l..r]$"*). Before attempting the seven blind problems below, study the two primary Part IV **Decoy Pairs** and the decision flowchart.

### 1.1 Decoy Pair A: Non-Hereditary Substring Borders (`Ch 15`) vs. Center-Hereditary Substring Palindromes (`Ch 17`)

Both paradigms take a static string $S[1..N]$ and answer $Q$ online or offline queries on a substring $W = S[l..r]$ ($N, Q \le 2 \times 10^5$). Why does Range Longest Palindromic Substring (`Range LPS`) admit a **true $O(1)$ query** via Sparse Table RMQ, whereas Range Longest Proper Border (`[BJWC2018]`) requires $O(\log N)$ dyadic Internal Pattern Matching (`IPM`) or $O(\log^2 N)$ Link-Tree HLD?

| Diagnostic Dimension | `Ch 15` Paradigm (`T-2B-04`: Dyadic IPM & 6-Method Substring Borders) | `Ch 17` Paradigm (`T-3A-03`: Two-Boundary Unclipping & Midpoint Decoupling) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Hereditary vs. Boundary-Coupled Geometry** | **Two-boundary coupled (non-hereditary)**: A border $S[l..l+b-1] = S[r-b+1..r]$ compares the *left* boundary $l$ against the *right* boundary $r-b+1$. Shifting $[l, r]$ changes **both** compared substrings simultaneously! | **Center-hereditary**: A palindrome centered at half-integer $c \in [l, r]$ remains a palindrome when clipped to $[l, r]$; its valid radius is simply $\min\bigl(R_{\text{man}}[c],\, c - (2l-1) + 1,\, (2r-1) - c + 1\bigr)$. |
| **Governing Combinatorial Invariant** | **Bounded-Ratio IPM AP Theorem**: For $b \in [2^m, 2^{m+1}-1]$, $b$ is a valid border of $S[l..r]$ iff $i = r - b + 1$ lies in the **intersection of two 1D APs**: $\operatorname{Occ}(P_m, S[r-2^{m+1}+2..r])$ and $\operatorname{Occ}(Q_m, S[l..l+2^{m+1}-2])$. | **Two-Boundary Unclipping Theorem**: Let $c_L$ be the center of the longest palindromic prefix of $S[l..r]$ and $c_R$ the center of its longest palindromic suffix. Every center $c \in (c_L, c_R)$ lies **100% unclipped** inside $[l, r]$! |
| **Suffix Comparison & Tie-Breaking** | Truncating $\operatorname{suf}(i)$ and $\operatorname{suf}(j)$ at $r$ flips their global SA order $\operatorname{rk}[i] < \operatorname{rk}[j]$ **iff** $S[j..r]$ is a proper prefix-border of $S[i..r]$. | Palindromic prefixes/suffixes of $S[l..r]$ are ancestor states of $\operatorname{first}[l]$ in $\operatorname{PAM}(S^R)$ and $\operatorname{last}[r]$ in $\operatorname{PAM}(S)$, found via `slink` ceiling division. |
| **Fatal Misdiagnosis** | Testing only whether $P_m = S[l..l+2^m-1]$ occurs in the tail window without intersecting the symmetric suffix AP of $Q_m$ (fails on $W = \texttt{ababacababab}$, `BP-4-01`). | Using a single midpoint $m = \lfloor(l+r)/2\rfloor$ for both odd and even Manacher centers in range multiplicity queries (misclassifies even center $m + 0.5$, `BP-4-05`). |

### 1.2 Decoy Pair B: Online 4-Way Deque / Tree PAM (`Ch 16`) vs. Static Range `slink` Telescoping & Rich Words (`Ch 17`)

Both paradigms track distinct palindromes and palindromic lengths across changing intervals $[L, R]$ of a string or tree. How do you decide between an online `Deque PAM` (`Ch 16`), an offline/persistent `slink` Telescoping Fenwick/Segment Tree (`Ch 17`), and a $O(N)$ Queue PAM two-pointer threshold (`Ch 17` Rich Words)?

| Diagnostic Dimension | `Ch 16` Paradigm (`T-3A-01` / `T-3A-02`: Unamortized Tree & 4-Way Deque PAM) | `Ch 17` Paradigm (`T-3A-04` / `T-3A-05`: `slink` Telescoping & Rich Word Closure) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Mutation vs. Random-Access Query Regime** | **Incremental endpoint mutations or tree branching**: The active string $S[L..R]$ changes by $\pm 1$ character at either end (`push_front`, `push_back`, `pop_front`, `pop_back`) or branches on a version tree. | **Arbitrary random-access range queries $[l, r]$**: Both endpoints $l$ and $r$ jump arbitrarily across $S[1..N]$ in each query. |
| **Why Amortized / Naive Updates Collapse** | On a tree or under `pop`, amortized `while` fail walks take $\Theta(N)$ per step, and popping $S[R]$ removes the boundary suffix $u = \operatorname{max\_suff}[R]$. | At right endpoint $r$, up to $\Theta(N)$ ancestors of $\operatorname{pos}[r]$ in the PAM fail tree acquire a new latest occurrence ending at $r$. |
| **Governing Combinatorial Invariant** | **Uniform Preceding-Character Lemma** (`quick_link[u][c]` in $O(1)$ or `slink`-skip in $O(\log N)$) + **Unique Vanishing Palindrome & Lazy Surface Push-Down** (`max_pref[l_u] <- fail[u]` in $O(1)$ without cascading!). | **Periodic Suffix Telescoping**: Along any `slink` chain $u_1 \to \dots \to u_k$, $\operatorname{start}_{r-1}(u_j) = \operatorname{start}_r(u_{j-1})$ ($2 \le j \le k$), so intermediate $+1/-1$ updates **cancel**! And for **Rich Words**, **Factor Closure** reduces range richness to $l \ge L_{\text{rich}}[r]$ in $O(1)$! |
| **Fatal Misdiagnosis** | Physically deleting PAM Trie nodes on `pop_back()` or cascading `fail` updates below $f = \operatorname{fail}[u]$ (`BP-4-03`, `BP-4-04`). | Building a heavy $O(N \log^2 N)$ `slink` telescoping structure to test whether $S[l..r]$ is a Rich Word when Factor Closure solves it in $O(N)$ preprocess + $O(1)$ query (`BP-4-07`). |

## 2. Unspoiled Blind Checkpoint Problems (`CP-IV-01` – `CP-IV-07`)

---

### Problem `CP-IV-01` — Truncated Substring Minimum Suffix & Length-Capped Self-Overlap

You are given a string $S[1..N]$ of lowercase English letters ($1 \le N \le 2 \times 10^5$) and $Q$ online queries ($1 \le Q \le 2 \times 10^5$). Each query specifies a substring $W = S[l..r]$ and a length cap $K$ ($1 \le K \le r - l$), and asks for **two** structural quantities of $W = S[l..r]$:

1. **Minimum Truncated Suffix**: Find the starting index $i^* \in [l, r]$ that minimizes the truncated suffix $S[i..r]$ in standard lexicographical order (if two indices produce identical strings, which is impossible since their lengths $r - i + 1$ differ, no tie occurs).
2. **Length-Capped Self-Overlap**: Find the largest integer $b \in [0, K]$ such that the length-$b$ prefix $S[l .. l+b-1]$ equals the length-$b$ suffix $S[r-b+1 .. r]$.

- **Constraints**: $1 \le N, Q \le 2 \times 10^5$, Online Queries, Time Limit $2.5\text{ s}$, Memory Limit $512\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}

- **Decoy Elimination (`Ch 15` vs. `Ch 17` Decoy Pair)**: Neither part involves mirror reversal ($S = S^R$). Moreover, in Part 1, why can't you simply return $i_0 = \arg\min_{i \in [l, r]} \operatorname{rk}[i]$ from the global Suffix Array of $S[1..N]$?
  - *Counterexample*: On $S = \texttt{abad}$ and $[l, r] = [1, 3]$ ($W = \texttt{aba}$), globally $\operatorname{suf}(1) = \texttt{abad} < \operatorname{suf}(3) = \texttt{ad}$ ($\operatorname{rk}[1] < \operatorname{rk}[3]$), yet inside $W = \texttt{aba}$, truncating at $r = 3$ gives $S[3..3] = \texttt{a} < S[1..3] = \texttt{aba}$!
- **Diagnostic Signal**: When does truncating $\operatorname{suf}(i)$ and $\operatorname{suf}(j)$ at $r$ flip their global Suffix Array order ($\operatorname{rk}[i] < \operatorname{rk}[j]$ globally, yet $S[j..r] <_{\text{lex}} S[i..r]$ locally)? **If and only if** $\operatorname{LCE}(i, j) \ge r - j + 1$—which means $j > i$ and $S[j..r]$ is a **proper prefix (and therefore a proper border!)** of $S[i..r]$! Thus both Part 1 and Part 2 are governed by **`Ch 15`'s Dyadic Bounded-Ratio Internal Pattern Matching (`T-2B-04`)**!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}

1. **For Part 1 (Truncated Minimum Suffix via Dyadic Prefix-Border Tie-Breaking)**:
   Let $i \in [l, r]$ be our current best candidate and $j \in (i, r]$ be a shorter candidate in scale $m$ where $r - j + 1 \in [2^m, 2^{m+1}-1]$. For $S[j..r]$ to beat $S[i..r]$, $S[j..r]$ must be a proper prefix of $S[i..r]$—so in particular $P_m = S[i .. i + 2^m - 1]$ must occur at starting position $j \in [r - 2^{m+1} + 2, \; r - 2^m + 1]$.
   By the **Bounded-Ratio IPM AP Theorem (`Ch 15` Theorem 15.2)**, all occurrences of $P_m$ inside the tail window $T_m = S[r - 2^{m+1} + 2 .. r]$ (of length $2^{m+1}-1 < 2|P_m|$) form a single arithmetic progression of step $d = \operatorname{per}(P_m)$! And among any arithmetic progression of occurrences of $P_m$ that are prefixes of $S[i..r]$, which one gives the lexicographically smallest truncated suffix $S[j..r]$? By periodicity on the overlapping core, **only the first (leftmost) occurrence $j_{\min}$ of $P_m$ in $[r - 2^{m+1} + 2, \; r - 2^m + 1]$** (or the shortest border in each AP) ever needs to be compared against $i$!

2. **For Part 2 (Length-Capped Border $b \in [1, K]$ via Two-Sided AP Intersection)**:
   In each dyadic scale $m \le \lfloor \log_2 K \rfloor$ where $b \in [2^m, \min(K, 2^{m+1}-1)]$:

   - Let $P_m = S[l .. l + 2^m - 1]$ and find its occurrence AP $\mathcal{A}_P$ inside $S[r - \min(K, 2^{m+1}-1) + 1 .. r]$;
   - Let $Q_m = S[r - 2^m + 1 .. r]$ and find its occurrence AP $\mathcal{A}_Q$ inside $S[l .. l + \min(K, 2^{m+1}-1) - 1]$.
   Since $2^m + 2^m > b$, $S[l..l+b-1] = S[r-b+1..r]$ holds **if and only if** $b$ belongs to both the shifted AP of $\mathcal{A}_P$ and the shifted AP of $\mathcal{A}_Q$!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}

1. Build the Suffix Array $\text{SA}[1..N]$, inverse rank $\text{rk}[1..N]$, $O(1)$ LCE RMQ, and a **Persistent Segment Tree (Chairman Tree)** over $\text{SA}[1..N]$ (storing minimum and maximum string index in each SA range) in $O(N \log N)$ time.
2. **Answering Part 1 in $O(\log^2 N)$**:
   - Start with $i^* = \text{SA}[\min_{k \in [l, r]} \text{rk}[k]]$ (the globally smallest suffix starting in $[l, r]$).
   - For each scale $m = \lfloor \log_2(r - l) \rfloor$ down to $0$: find the SA interval $[L_m, R_m]$ of $P_m = S[i^* .. i^* + 2^m - 1]$ via RMQ binary search around $\text{rk}[i^*]$, query the Chairman Tree on $[L_m, R_m]$ for the **largest** (or smallest valid border) index $j \in [\max(i^* + 1, r - 2^{m+1} + 2), \; r - 2^m + 1]$, and update $i^* \leftarrow \arg\min_{\text{trunc}}(i^*, j)$ via an $O(1)$ truncated LCE comparison!
3. **Answering Part 2 in $O(\log^2 N)$**:
   - Iterate $m = \lfloor \log_2 K \rfloor$ down to $0$ (stopping as soon as a valid $b$ is found). In scale $m$, extract at most 3 points (min, 2nd min, max) of $\mathcal{A}_P$ in $[r - \min(K, 2^{m+1}-1) + 1, \; r - 2^m + 1]$ via the Chairman Tree over $[L(P_m), R(P_m)]$. Either verify the $\le 2$ points directly via $\operatorname{LCE}(l, r - b + 1) \ge b$, or intersect $\mathcal{A}_P$ with $\mathcal{A}_Q$ in $O(1)$ time!
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-IV-01"}

- **Target Chapter & Technique ID**: **[Chapter 15](../chapters/ch15-internal-pattern-matching-borders.qmd) (`T-2B-04`: Kociumaka's Basic Substring Dictionary, Bounded-Ratio IPM Single-AP Theorem & Two-Sided Dyadic Border AP Intersection; Decoy Pair A · Part 1 / `[ZJOI2017] 字符串` & `[BJWC2018] Border 的四种求法`)**.
- **Proof of the One-Sided $P_m$ Failure & Two-Sided $P_m \cap Q_m$ Exact Coverage**:
  Why is checking $P_m = S[l..l+2^m-1]$ alone insufficient in Part 2 unless you also verify $\operatorname{LCE}(l, r-b+1) \ge b$ or intersect with $Q_m = S[r-2^m+1..r]$?
  Consider the canonical counterexample $W = \texttt{ababacababab}$ of length $12$ at scale $m = 2$ ($2^m = 4$) testing candidate border $b = 6$:

  - The prefix $P_2 = W[1..4] = \texttt{abab}$ occurs at $i = 12 - 6 + 1 = 7$ because $W[7..10] = \texttt{abab}$!
  - Yet $b = 6$ is **not** a border of $W$ because $W[1..6] = \texttt{ababac} \ne \texttt{ababab} = W[7..12]$ (mismatch at $W[6] = \texttt{c} \ne \texttt{b} = W[12]$)!
  When we intersect with the suffix check $Q_2 = W[9..12] = \texttt{abab}$ occurring at $l + b - 2^m = 3$ ($W[3..6] = \texttt{abac} \ne \texttt{abab}$), $b = 6$ is immediately rejected! Because $2^m + 2^m \ge b + 1$ for every $b \in [2^m, 2^{m+1}-1]$, the head check $P_m$ (first $2^m$ chars) and tail check $Q_m$ (last $2^m$ chars) cover 100% of the candidate border with zero unverified middle characters.

- **Boundary Pitfall Audit (`BP-4-01`, `BP-4-02`)**:
  - **One-Sided $P_m$ Check Without $Q_m$ Intersection (`BP-4-01`)**: Never accept an AP from $\mathcal{A}_P$ alone when $|\mathcal{A}_P| \ge 3$; either intersect $\mathcal{A}_P$ with $\mathcal{A}_Q$, or clamp the periodic continuation of $P_m$ at $l$ against $\operatorname{LCE}(l, l + d)$ and at $r$ against $\operatorname{LCSuf}(r, r - d)$.
  - **Small-AP Step Extrapolation (`BP-4-02`)**: Theorem 15.2 guarantees step $d = x_2 - x_1 = \operatorname{per}(P_m)$ **only when the AP has $\ge 3$ elements**! When $|\mathcal{A}_P| \le 2$, two occurrences of $P_m$ can overlap by less than $2^m - \operatorname{per}(P_m)$ (a non-periodic border of $P_m$), so always test the $\le 2$ candidate lengths directly in $O(1)$ via $\operatorname{LCE}(l, r - b + 1) \ge b$.
- **Complexity**: $O(N \log N)$ preprocessing and $O(\log^2 N)$ time per query, in $O(N \log N)$ space.
::::

### Problem `CP-IV-02` — Memory-Bounded Substring Palindromic Margins & Peak Length

You are given a string $S[1..N]$ of lowercase letters ($1 \le N \le 3 \times 10^5$) and $Q$ online queries $[l, r]$ ($1 \le Q \le 3 \times 10^5$) under a **strict $64\text{ MB}$ memory limit**.

For each query substring $W = S[l..r]$, compute three quantities:

1. $|P_L(l, r)|$: the length of the **longest palindromic prefix** of $S[l..r]$;
2. $|P_R(l, r)|$: the length of the **longest palindromic suffix** of $S[l..r]$;
3. $\operatorname{LPS}(l, r)$: the length of the **longest palindromic substring** anywhere inside $S[l..r]$, evaluated **without** binary searching the answer length!

- **Constraints**: $1 \le N, Q \le 3 \times 10^5$, Online Queries, Time Limit $1.5\text{ s}$, **Memory Limit $64\text{ MB}$**.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}

- **Decoy Elimination (`Ch 17` vs. `Ch 15` Decoy Pair)**: Compare this directly against `CP-IV-01`:
  - In `CP-IV-01`, general borders of $S[l..r]$ are **not** suffixes of $S[1..r]$ in any single border tree, requiring 2D Persistent Segment Trees ($O(N \log N)$ words, exceeding $64\text{ MB}$!).
  - Here, every palindromic suffix of $S[l..r]$ is also a palindromic suffix of the prefix $S[1..r]$! Specifically, $P_R(l, r)$ is simply the **longest ancestor $v$ of $u_0 = \operatorname{last}[r]$ in $\operatorname{PAM}(S)$ satisfying $\operatorname{len}[v] \le r - l + 1$** (and symmetrically, $P_L(l, r)$ is the longest ancestor of $\operatorname{first}[l]$ in $\operatorname{PAM}(S^R)$ with $\operatorname{len}[v] \le r - l + 1$)!
- **Diagnostic Signal**: Because the $64\text{ MB}$ limit forbids a $20 \times 3 \times 10^5$ binary-lifting table on $\operatorname{PAM}(S)$ and $\operatorname{PAM}(S^R)$, how do we locate the highest ancestor of $u_0 = \operatorname{last}[r]$ with $\operatorname{len}[v] \le r - l + 1$ using only $O(N)$ PAM memory, and how do $P_L(l, r)$ and $P_R(l, r)$ immediately unlock $\operatorname{LPS}(l, r)$ via a single RMQ lookup?
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}

1. **Closed-Form `slink` Ceiling Division (`Ch 17` Invariant B / `T-3A-03`)**:
   Start at $u = \operatorname{last}[r]$ in $\operatorname{PAM}(S)$ and walk $u \leftarrow \operatorname{slink}[u]$ while $\operatorname{len}[\operatorname{slink}[u]] > r - l + 1$ (at most $\lceil \log_2(r-l+1) \rceil$ hops, typically $\le 3$ hops!). Now $\operatorname{len}[\operatorname{slink}[u]] \le r - l + 1$. If $\operatorname{len}[u] > r - l + 1$, the target ancestor lies inside $u$'s arithmetic progression of step $d = \operatorname{diff}[u]$, so its exact length is given in $O(1)$ closed form by:
   $$|P_R(l, r)| = \operatorname{len}[u] - \left\lceil \frac{\operatorname{len}[u] - (r - l + 1)}{\operatorname{diff}[u]} \right\rceil \cdot \operatorname{diff}[u]!$$
   Applying the exact same formula on $\operatorname{PAM}(S^R)$ from $\operatorname{first}[l]$ gives $|P_L(l, r)|$ using **$O(N)$ PAM memory**!

2. **The Two-Boundary Unclipping Identity for Range LPS (`Ch 17` Theorem 17.1 / `T-3A-03`)**:
   In the $2N-1$ half-integer Manacher center coordinates $c \in \{1, 2, \dots, 2N-1\}$ (where original index $i$ is at $2i - 1$):

   - The longest palindromic prefix $P_L = S[l .. l + |P_L| - 1]$ is centered at $c_L = (2l - 1) + |P_L| - 1$.
   - The longest palindromic suffix $P_R = S[r - |P_R| + 1 .. r]$ is centered at $c_R = (2r - 1) - |P_R| + 1$.
   **Unclipped Interior Center Theorem**: No center $c \in (c_L, c_R)$ can have its whole-string Manacher palindrome touch or cross $l$ (else it would form a palindromic prefix of $S[l..r]$ longer than $P_L$, since $c > c_L$!) nor touch or cross $r$ (else it would form a palindromic suffix longer than $P_R$, since $c < c_R$!). Therefore:
   $$\operatorname{LPS}(l, r) = \max\!\Bigl(\,|P_L(l, r)|,\;\; |P_R(l, r)|,\;\; \max_{c_L < c < c_R} \operatorname{ManacherLen}[c]\,\Bigr)!$$
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}

1. To stay well inside $64\text{ MB}$ for $N = 3 \times 10^5$:
   - Store PAM transitions using a compact first-child / next-sibling linked list (`head[u], nxt[u], ch[u]`) instead of `tr[u][26]`, so both $\operatorname{PAM}(S)$ and $\operatorname{PAM}(S^R)$ take $< 15\text{ MB}$ total!
   - Compute the unified Manacher length array $M[1..2N-1]$ in $O(N)$ time, and build a **Block-RMQ (or byte-packed / $B=16$ micro-block Sparse Table)** over $M[1..2N-1]$ in $< 8\text{ MB}$!
2. For each query $[l, r]$:
   - Compute $|P_L(l, r)|$ on $\operatorname{PAM}(S^R)$ and $|P_R(l, r)|$ on $\operatorname{PAM}(S)$ via `slink` ceiling division.
   - Set $c_L = 2l - 2 + |P_L|$ and $c_R = 2r - |P_R|$.
   - If $c_L + 1 \le c_R - 1$, query $\max_{c \in [c_L+1, c_R-1]} M[c]$ in $O(1)$ time and take the maximum with $|P_L|$ and $|P_R|$.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-IV-02"}

- **Target Chapter & Technique ID**: **[Chapter 17](../chapters/ch17-range-palindromes-rich-words.qmd) (`T-3A-03`: Closed-Form `slink` Ceiling Division & Two-Boundary Unclipping Theorem for Range LPS; Decoy Pair A · Part 2)**.
- **How to Achieve True Worst-Case $O(1)$ Per Query When Memory Allows**:
  As shown in `Ch 17` Theorem 17.1, notice that $c_L$ is the **rightmost** Manacher center $\le 2r - 1$ whose left Manacher endpoint $L_{\text{man}}[c] \le 2l - 1$ (namely $c_L = \text{rightmost\_reach}[2l - 1]$ when $c_L \le c_R$!), and $c_R$ is the **leftmost** Manacher center $\ge 2l - 1$ whose right Manacher endpoint $R_{\text{man}}[c] \ge 2r - 1$ ($c_R = \text{leftmost\_reach}[2r - 1]$)!
  Precomputing `rightmost_reach[1..2N-1]` and `leftmost_reach[1..2N-1]` by two linear sweeps over the Manacher intervals finds $c_L$ and $c_R$ in **true $O(1)$ time without even building a PAM** whenever $c_L \le c_R$ (and when $c_L > c_R$, the two boundary palindromes cross the midpoint $m = l + r - 1$, so clamping $c_L \leftarrow \min(c_L, m)$ or reading the midpoint split still takes $O(1)$ time!).

- **Boundary Pitfall Audit (`BP-4-06`)**:
  - **Including $c_L$ or $c_R$ Inside the Unclipped RMQ Range $[c_L, c_R]$**: The whole-string Manacher palindrome at $c_L$ itself *can* extend strictly to the left of $l$ (and $c_R$ can extend strictly to the right of $r$). Their valid clipped lengths inside $S[l..r]$ are already accounted for by $|P_L| = c_L - (2l - 1) + 1$ and $|P_R| = (2r - 1) - c_R + 1$. You **must** query the open interior $[c_L + 1, c_R - 1]$!
- **Complexity**: $O(N)$ (or $O(N \log N)$) preprocessing, $O(\log N)$ via `slink` ceiling division or **true $O(1)$** via boundary reach arrays per query, in $< 25\text{ MB}$ space.
::::

### Problem `CP-IV-03` — Cross-Window Palindromic Witness Search

You are given a string $S[1..N]$ of lowercase letters ($1 \le N \le 10^5$) and $Q$ online queries ($1 \le Q \le 10^5$). Each query provides four indices $(a, b, c, d)$ ($1 \le a \le b \le N$, $1 \le c \le d \le N$) and asks for the **maximum length of a palindromic substring** of $S[a..b]$ that **also occurs as a substring** inside $S[c..d]$ (or `0` if no non-empty palindrome appears in both windows).

- **Constraints**: $1 \le N, Q \le 10^5$, Online Queries, Time Limit $2.0\text{ s}$, Memory Limit $512\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}

- **Decoy Elimination**: Do not confuse this with standard `[HEOI2016 / TJOI2016] 字符串` (`Ch 10` / `Ch 15`), where the candidate substring must start at $c$. Here, the candidate $P$ can sit *anywhere* inside $S[a..b]$ AND *anywhere* inside $S[c..d]$, subject to $P = P^R$ being a **palindrome**!
- **Diagnostic Signal**: Why is a general 4-parameter common substring query $\operatorname{LCS}(S[a..b], S[c..d])$ much harder than the **palindromic** version?
  1. Every distinct palindrome $u$ in $S$ is a node of $\operatorname{PAM}(S)$, and $u$ occurs inside $S[c..d]$ **if and only if** $u$'s right-endpoint set $\operatorname{endpos}_{\text{PAM}}(u)$ in the **PAM `fail` tree** intersects $[c + \operatorname{len}[u] - 1, \; d]$!
  2. Furthermore, the predicate $\operatorname{HasCommonPal}_{\ge L}(a, b, c, d)$ on center radius is **monotone** under two-sided center stripping AND under `fail`-tree ancestry: if a palindrome $u$ occurs in $S[c..d]$, then **every `fail`-ancestor (palindromic border) AND every center-shrunk sub-palindrome of $u$** also occurs in $S[c..d]$!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}
Look at any palindrome $P = S[x..y] \subseteq S[a..b]$ with PAM node $u$:

- **Containment in $S[c..d]$ via PAM Fail-Tree Segment Tree Merging**:
  By merging dynamic segment trees bottom-up along the **PAM `fail` tree** (exactly like SAM link-tree $\operatorname{endpos}$ merging in `Ch 10`, except on $\operatorname{PAM}(S)$!), we can test in $O(\log N)$ time whether a PAM node $u$ occurs in $S[c..d]$ by checking:
  $$\operatorname{SegTree\_Query}\bigl(\operatorname{root}[u],\; c + \operatorname{len}[u] - 1,\; d\bigr) > 0.$$

- **How to Locate the Maximal Valid Palindrome Centered at $m$ or Ending at $r$**:
  For every half-integer center $m \in [1, 2N-1]$ in $S$, let $u_{\max}(m)$ be the PAM node of the maximal whole-string Manacher palindrome centered at $m$. In the **PAM Trie** (where parent edge strips the outer two characters $x \cdot p \cdot x \to p$), every palindrome centered at $m$ is a **Trie ancestor** of $u_{\max}(m)$!
  Even better: along the root-to-$u_{\max}(m)$ path in the **PAM Trie**, the condition *"occurs in $S[c..d]$ and has length $\le \text{clip}(m, a, b)$"* is **100% monotone in Trie depth**! Specifically, for each PAM node $u$, let $\operatorname{first\_occ}(u, c, d)$ be the minimum right endpoint of $u$ in $[c + \operatorname{len}[u] - 1, d]$. Equivalently, for each right endpoint $y \in [c, d]$, the longest palindrome ending at $y$ that fits inside $S[c..y]$ and also occurs in $S[a..b]$ is a `fail`-ancestor of $\operatorname{last}[y]$!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}

1. Build $\operatorname{PAM}(S)$ and perform **Segment Tree Merging** bottom-up over the **PAM `fail` tree** in $O(N \log N)$ time and space, so every PAM node $u$ has a persistent segment tree $\operatorname{root}[u]$ over its right endpoints $\operatorname{endpos}(u) \subseteq [1, N]$.
2. By `Ch 17` Invariant A, stripping the outer character pair from a palindrome of length $\ge 2k - 1$ centered at $m \in [a + k - 1, b - k + 1]$ preserves both its center $m$ and its occurrence inside $S[c..d]$.
3. Even more directly: in $S[a..b]$, apply `Ch 17`'s **Two-Boundary Unclipping (`CP-IV-02`)**! Every maximal palindrome inside $S[a..b]$ is either:
   - The longest palindromic prefix $P_L(a, b)$ or longest palindromic suffix $P_R(a, b)$ (for which we walk `slink` / binary-lift on the PAM `fail` tree to find the longest ancestor $u$ whose $\operatorname{root}[u]$ intersects $[c + \operatorname{len}[u] - 1, d]$), or
   - Centered at an unclipped interior center $m \in (a_L, a_R)$ (or symmetrically, an unclipped center $m' \in (c_L, c_R)$ inside $S[c..d]$ tested against $[a + \operatorname{len}[u] - 1, b]$, plus boundary-clipped prefixes/suffixes of $S[c..d]$ tested against $S[a..b]$!).
4. Specifically, if $P$ is a longest common palindrome of $S[a..b]$ and $S[c..d]$, then at least one of its occurrences in $S[a..b]$ or $S[c..d]$ cannot be expanded outward by $+1$ on both sides—meaning $P$ is either a boundary palindrome ($P_L$ or $P_R$) of one of the two windows, or a full whole-string Manacher palindrome $u_{\max}(m)$ (or the PAM Trie ancestor lifted against $\operatorname{endpos}$)!
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-IV-03"}

- **Target Chapter & Technique ID**: **[Chapter 16](../chapters/ch16-deterministic-tree-deque-pam.qmd) & [Chapter 17](../chapters/ch17-range-palindromes-rich-words.qmd) (`T-3A-03`: Two-Boundary Unclipping Duality Coupled with PAM Fail-Tree $\operatorname{endpos}$ Segment Tree Merge, `W3A-27` / `[ZJOI2016 / HEOI2016]` Palindromic Dual)**.
- **Proof of the Symmetrized Boundary + Unclipped Interior Reduction**:
  Suppose $P$ (corresponding to PAM node $u$) is a maximum-length palindromic substring occurring in both $S[a..b]$ and $S[c..d]$. In $\operatorname{PAM}(S)$, $u$ occurs in $S[c..d]$ iff $\operatorname{SegTree\_Query}(\operatorname{root}[u], c + \operatorname{len}[u] - 1, d) > 0$.
  Moreover, because occurrence in $S[c..d]$ is hereditary along both the PAM **Trie** (shrinking around a fixed center $m$) and the PAM **`fail` tree** (taking palindromic borders at a fixed boundary):

  1. For each center $m \in [1, 2N - 1]$, let $u_{\max}(m)$ be its whole-string Manacher node in $\operatorname{PAM}(S)$. Pre-link the PAM Trie with binary lifting `trie_up[u][k]` (or HLD).
  2. Using two-boundary unclipping (`CP-IV-02`) on both $S[a..b]$ and $S[c..d]$, any common palindrome that touches $a, b, c,$ or $d$ is found in $O(\log^2 N)$ by lifting $P_L(a, b), P_R(a, b)$ against $\operatorname{endpos}$ in $[c, d]$ and lifting $P_L(c, d), P_R(c, d)$ against $\operatorname{endpos}$ in $[a, b]$. And any common palindrome strictly inside $(a_L, a_R)$ and $(c_L, c_R)$ is bounded by the unclipped centers or binary search on radius $k$!
- **Boundary Pitfall Audit (`BP-4-06`)**:
  - **Merging Segment Trees on the PAM Trie Instead of the PAM `fail` Tree**: A palindrome $u$'s occurrences in $S$ are inherited from its suffixes in the **`fail` tree** (`fail[w] = u`), *not* from its extensions $c u c$ in the PAM Trie. Always merge $\operatorname{endpos}$ segment trees bottom-up along the **`fail` tree**, and apply open-interior two-boundary unclipping (`BP-4-06`).
- **Complexity**: $O((N + Q) \log^2 N)$ time and $O(N \log N)$ space.

### Problem `CP-IV-04` — Encrypted Four-Way Deque Palindromic Defect & Boundary Split Stream

You maintain a dynamic string $W = S[L..R]$ (initially empty, with $L = 1, R = 0$ centered inside a buffer of size $2Q + 10$) across $Q$ online **encrypted** operations ($1 \le Q \le 4 \times 10^5$) of four types:

1. `push_front(c)`: prepend lowercase letter $c$ to the left end ($L \leftarrow L - 1, S[L] = c$);
2. `push_back(c)`: append lowercase letter $c$ to the right end ($R \leftarrow R + 1, S[R] = c$);
3. `pop_front()`: remove the leftmost character $S[L]$ ($L \leftarrow L + 1$, guaranteed $L \le R$);
4. `pop_back()`: remove the rightmost character $S[R]$ ($R \leftarrow R - 1$, guaranteed $L \le R$).

After each operation, let $|W| = R - L + 1$ be the current length and $|\operatorname{Pal}^+(W)|$ be the number of **distinct non-empty palindromic substrings** currently present in $W$. Output two integers (which also decrypt the next operation's character $c'$ via $c = (c' \oplus \text{ans}) \bmod 26$):

- The **palindromic defect** $\delta(W) = |W| - |\operatorname{Pal}^+(W)|$, and
- The sum of the lengths of the longest palindromic prefix and longest palindromic suffix of $W$.

- **Constraints**: $1 \le Q \le 4 \times 10^5$, Strictly Online Encrypted Operations, Time Limit $1.5\text{ s}$, Memory Limit $256\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}

- **Decoy Elimination (`Ch 16` vs. `Ch 17` Decoy Pair)**: Because the operations are **strictly online and encrypted**, you cannot pre-simulate the deque to build a static string and run `Ch 17`'s offline `slink` telescoping (`CP-IV-05`). Conversely, because both `pop_front()` and `pop_back()` occur arbitrarily (not LIFO stack undo), you cannot simply roll back a history stack! This requires **`Ch 16`'s Full 4-Way Double-Ended Deque PAM (`T-3A-01` & `T-3A-02`)** in worst-case $O(1)$ time per step.
- **Diagnostic Signal**: Three things break in a standard amortized PAM when you support 4-way deque operations:
  1. Repeating `push_back('b')` + `pop_back()` on $W = \texttt{a}^{Q/2}$ forces the standard `while` fail walk to take $\Theta(Q)$ steps per push ($\Theta(Q^2)$ TLE);
  2. Popping $S[R]$ invalidates `max_suff[R]`, and we must know whether that palindrome still occurs elsewhere in $S[L..R-1]$;
  3. After popping $S[R]$, what is the new longest palindromic suffix of $S[L..R-1]$ ending at $R - 1$?
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}
Three invariants from `Ch 16` resolve all three bottlenecks in **worst-case $O(1)$ time**:

1. **Unamortized Direct Fail Link (`quick_link[u][c]` — `T-3A-01`)**:
   For any PAM node $u$ with $f = \operatorname{fail}[u]$ and preceding internal character $c_0 = P_u[\operatorname{len}[f] + 1] = S[r - 1 - \operatorname{len}[f]]$:
   $$\operatorname{quick\_link}[u][c] = \begin{cases} f & \text{if } c = c_0, \\ \operatorname{quick\_link}[f][c] & \text{if } c \ne c_0. \end{cases}$$
   Checking $S[R - 1 - \operatorname{len}[u]] == c$ first and otherwise jumping $u \leftarrow \operatorname{quick\_link}[u][c]$ finds the fail parent in **strictly $O(1)$ worst-case time**!

2. **Unique Vanishing Palindrome Theorem (`T-3A-02`)**:
   When `pop_back()` deletes $S[R]$, let $u = \operatorname{max\_suff}[R]$. Every proper `fail`-ancestor $v$ of $u$ is a proper border of the palindrome $u$, so its **reflected prefix copy** inside $u$ occupies $S[R - \operatorname{len}[u] + 1 .. R - \operatorname{len}[u] + \operatorname{len}[v]] \subseteq S[L .. R - 1]$! Thus **no proper ancestor of $u$ can vanish from $S[L..R-1]$**; at most the single node $u = \operatorname{max\_suff}[R]$ can disappear!

3. **Non-Cascading Lazy Surface Push-Down (`T-3A-02`)**:
   Maintain `max_pref[i]` and `max_suff[i]` for $i \in [L, R]$, `surf_cnt[u]` (number of active boundary pointers `max_pref[i]` or `max_suff[i]` pointing to $u$), and `deg[u]` (number of active PAM nodes $w$ with $\operatorname{fail}[w] = u$). A node $u$ ($\operatorname{len}[u] > 0$) exists in $S[L..R]$ iff $\operatorname{surf\_cnt}[u] + \operatorname{deg}[u] > 0$.
   On `pop_back()` at $R$: let $u = \operatorname{max\_suff}[R]$, $l_u = R - \operatorname{len}[u] + 1$, and $f = \operatorname{fail}[u]$. Clear `max_suff[R]`, set $\operatorname{max\_pref}[l_u] \leftarrow \max_{\text{len}}(\operatorname{max\_pref}[l_u], f)$, and set $\operatorname{max\_suff}[l_u + \operatorname{len}[f] - 1] \leftarrow \max_{\text{len}}(\dots, f)$!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}

1. **Permanent PAM Trie Reuse**: Never delete or unlink `tr[p][c]` when a node's active count drops to $0$! If the same palindrome is formed again later, reuse the existing node ID $u$ and increment `active_distinct` when $\operatorname{surf\_cnt}[u] + \operatorname{deg}[u]$ transitions from $0 \to >0$ (simultaneously incrementing $\operatorname{deg}[\operatorname{fail}[u]]$).
2. **Whole-String Crossover Synchronization**:
   - On `push_back(c)`: find/create $u = \operatorname{max\_suff}[R]$ from $\operatorname{max\_suff}[R-1]$ using `quick_link`. Set $\operatorname{max\_pref}[R - \operatorname{len}[u] + 1] \leftarrow \max_{\text{len}}(\dots, u)$. If $\operatorname{len}[u] == R - L + 1$, $u$ spans the entire active deque, so $\operatorname{max\_pref}[L] = u$!
   - Symmetrically on `push_front(c)` using $\operatorname{max\_pref}[L+1]$.
3. **Why Deletions Never Cascade on `pop_back()` / `pop_front()`**:
   When pushing $f = \operatorname{fail}[u]$ onto $\operatorname{max\_pref}[l_u]$ and $\operatorname{max\_suff}[l_u + \operatorname{len}[f] - 1]$, perform those pointer assignments **before** checking whether $\operatorname{surf\_cnt}[u] + \operatorname{deg}[u] == 0$ (which decrements $\operatorname{deg}[f]$). Because $f$ just gained at least one surface reference at $\operatorname{max\_pref}[l_u]$, $\operatorname{surf\_cnt}[f] + \operatorname{deg}[f]$ is strictly positive and **never cascades**!

4. After each step, if $L > R$, both outputs are `0`; otherwise output $(R - L + 1) - \text{active\_distinct}$ and $\operatorname{len}[\operatorname{max\_pref}[L]] + \operatorname{len}[\operatorname{max\_suff}[R]]$.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-IV-04"}

- **Target Chapter & Technique ID**: **[Chapter 16](../chapters/ch16-deterministic-tree-deque-pam.qmd) (`T-3A-01` & `T-3A-02`: Unamortized `quick_link[u][c]`, Unique Vanishing Palindrome Theorem & Non-Cascading Lazy Surface Push-Down; Decoy Pair B · Part 1)**.
- **Why Lazy Surface Push-Down Guarantees Exact Boundary Pointers at $R - 1$**:
  Suppose `pop_back()` removes $S[R]$. How do we know that $\operatorname{max\_suff}[R - 1]$ already holds the true longest palindromic suffix of $S[L .. R - 1]$?
  Consider the true longest palindromic suffix $P^*$ of $S[L .. R - 1]$, starting at $l^* = (R - 1) - |P^*| + 1 \ge L$ and ending at $R - 1$:

  - Either $P^*$ was *already* the longest palindrome starting at $l^*$ (or ending at $R - 1$) when $l^*$ or $R - 1$ was pushed, in which case `max_suff[R - 1]` already has length $\ge |P^*|$;
  - Or $P^*$ was previously overshadowed at left endpoint $l^*$ by some longer palindrome $Q$ starting at $l^*$ that extended to some $r_Q \ge R$. Since $S[R .. r_Q]$ has now been popped by successive `pop_back()` calls, at the exact moment $r_Q$ was popped, lazy surface push-down replaced $Q$ at $l^*$ with $\operatorname{fail}[Q]$, and by induction pushed down along the border chain starting at $l^*$ until the longest border of $Q$ ending at $\le R - 1$—which is $P^*$ itself—was written into `max_suff[R - 1]`!
- **Boundary Pitfall Audit (`BP-4-03`, `BP-4-04`)**:
  - **Forgetting Whole-String Crossover (`BP-4-03`)**: When `push_back(c)` creates a palindrome of length $R - L + 1$, updating `max_pref[R - len[u] + 1]` automatically updates `max_pref[L]`! However, if you maintain separate scalar pointers `first` and `last` instead of reading `max_pref[L]` and `max_suff[R]`, forgetting `if (len[last] == R - L + 1) first = last;` corrupts the next `push_front`. Storing `max_pref[L..R]` and `max_suff[L..R]` directly eliminates separate `first`/`last` sync bugs!
  - **Out-of-Bounds Mirror Read (`BP-4-04`)**: Before `push_back(c)` at $R$, set sentinel $S[L - 1] = -1$; before `push_front(c)` at $L$, set sentinel $S[R + 1] = -1$. Otherwise $S[R - 1 - \operatorname{len}[u]]$ can match a stale character popped earlier at $L - 1$!
- **Complexity**: Worst-case $O(1)$ time per operation ($O(Q |\Sigma|)$ total time and space).
::::

### Problem `CP-IV-05` — Substring Palindromic Saturation vs. Length-Weighted Distinct Palindromes

For any string $W$ of length $|W|$, its number of distinct non-empty palindromic substrings satisfies $|\operatorname{Pal}^+(W)| \le |W|$ ($\delta(W) \ge 0$ in `CP-IV-04`). Call a string $W$ **palindromically saturated** if it achieves this theoretical maximum $|\operatorname{Pal}^+(W)| = |W|$ ($\delta(W) = 0$).

You are given a static string $S[1..N]$ of lowercase letters ($1 \le N \le 2.5 \times 10^5$) and $Q$ queries ($1 \le Q \le 2.5 \times 10^5$) of two types on a range $[l, r]$ ($1 \le l \le r \le N$):

- **Type 1 (`t = 1, l, r`)**: Count how many sub-intervals $[x, y] \subseteq [l, r]$ ($l \le x \le y \le r$) form a **palindromically saturated** substring $S[x..y]$.
- **Type 2 (`t = 2, l, r`)**: Compute **both** the number of distinct non-empty palindromic substrings in $S[l..r]$ **and** the sum of their lengths:
  $$C(l, r) = \bigl|\operatorname{Pal}^+(S[l..r])\bigr|, \qquad \Sigma_{\text{len}}(l, r) = \sum_{P \in \operatorname{Pal}^+(S[l..r])} |P|.$$

- **Constraints**: $1 \le N, Q \le 2.5 \times 10^5$, Time Limit $2.5\text{ s}$, Memory Limit $512\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}

- **Decoy Elimination (`Ch 17` Rich Word Factor Closure vs. `slink` Telescoping)**:
  - Why does Type 1 ask for the number of saturated sub-intervals $[x, y] \subseteq [l, r]$ over all $\binom{r-l+2}{2}$ pairs, whereas Type 2 asks for a *single* interval $[l, r]$?
  - If you try to solve Type 1 using Type 2's $O(\log^2 N)$ `slink` telescoping engine, evaluating all $\binom{r-l+2}{2}$ sub-intervals takes $\Theta(N^2 \log N)$ per query!
- **Diagnostic Signal**:
  1. A "palindromically saturated" string ($|\operatorname{Pal}^+(W)| = |W|$) is precisely a **Rich Word** (`Ch 17` / `T-3A-05`)! By the **Glen–Justin–Widmer–Zamboni Factor-Closure Theorem**, *every substring of a Rich Word is also a Rich Word*. Thus for each right endpoint $y \in [1, N]$, the valid left endpoints $x \le y$ form a contiguous interval $[L_{\text{rich}}[y], y]$ with a monotonically non-decreasing boundary $L_{\text{rich}}[1] \le L_{\text{rich}}[2] \le \dots \le L_{\text{rich}}[N]$!
  2. **Type 2 is governed by `[徐毅 2014]` PAM `slink` Periodic Suffix Telescoping (`Ch 17` Theorem 17.3 / `T-3A-04`)** generalized to both unweighted ($w(u) = 1$) and length-weighted ($w(u) = \operatorname{len}[u]$) distinct palindromes!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}

1. **Factor-Closure Two-Pointer Threshold $L_{\text{rich}}[1..N]$ (`T-3A-05`)**:
   Run a sliding-window Queue PAM (`push_back` + `pop_front` from `CP-IV-04`) across $y = 1, 2, \dots, N$: after pushing $S[y]$, while $\text{active\_distinct} < y - L + 1$, call `pop_front()` and increment $L$. Record $L_{\text{rich}}[y] = L$ in $O(N)$ total time!
   Then for any Type 1 query $[l, r]$, the number of rich sub-intervals $[x, y] \subseteq [l, r]$ is:
   $$\sum_{y=l}^r \bigl(y - \max(l, L_{\text{rich}}[y]) + 1\bigr),$$
   which splits at the binary-searched index $y_0 = \text{lower\_bound}(L_{\text{rich}}, l)$ into two $O(1)$ prefix-sum lookups!

2. **Unweighted & Length-Weighted `slink` Periodic Telescoping (`T-3A-04`)**:
   Sweep $r = 1, 2, \dots, N$. At step $r$, walk the $O(\log r)$ `slink` chains from $\operatorname{last}[r]$ to the root. For a chain $u_1 \to u_2 \to \dots \to u_k$ of common period $d = \operatorname{diff}[u_1]$ (where $u_k$ has $\operatorname{len}[u_k] = \operatorname{len}[\operatorname{slink}[u_1]] + d$):

   - Every non-head node $u_j$ ($2 \le j \le k$) had its previous occurrence at right endpoint **$r - d$**, so its old start position equals $u_{j-1}$'s new start position:
     $$\operatorname{start}_{r-1}(u_j) = (r - d) - \operatorname{len}[u_j] + 1 = r - \bigl(\operatorname{len}[u_j] + d\bigr) + 1 = r - \operatorname{len}[u_{j-1}] + 1 = \operatorname{start}_r(u_{j-1})!$$

   - **For Unweighted Count ($w(u) = 1$)**: All intermediate nodes $j \in [2, k]$ cancel ($+1 - 1 = 0$), leaving **one `-1` point update** at $\operatorname{prev\_r}(u_1) - \operatorname{len}[u_1] + 1$ and **one `+1` point update** at $r - \operatorname{len}[u_k] + 1$!
   - **For Length Sum ($w(u) = \operatorname{len}[u]$)**: Across the chain $\{u_1, \dots, u_k\}$, the net weight change is $-\operatorname{len}[u_1]$ at $\operatorname{prev\_r}(u_1) - \operatorname{len}[u_1] + 1$, $+\operatorname{len}[u_k]$ at $r - \operatorname{len}[u_k] + 1$, and a constant difference $+\bigl(\operatorname{len}[u_{j-1}] - \operatorname{len}[u_j]\bigr) = +d$ at each intermediate start position $r - \operatorname{len}[u_{j-1}] + 1$ ($2 \le j \le k$); or via **Link-Cut Tree `access(last[r])`** on the PAM `fail` tree, where each solid splay chain shares a uniform previous right endpoint $t_{\text{old}}$.
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}

1. **Type 1 ($O(N)$ Preprocess, $O(\log N)$ or $O(1)$ Query)**:
   - Compute $L_{\text{rich}}[1..N]$ via two-pointer Queue PAM in $O(N)$ time, and precompute prefix sums of $L_{\text{rich}}[y]$ and $y - L_{\text{rich}}[y] + 1$.
   - For query $[l, r]$, binary search the first $y_0 \in [l, r]$ with $L_{\text{rich}}[y_0] \ge l$; sub-intervals with $y < y_0$ contribute $\sum_{y=l}^{y_0-1} (y - l + 1)$, and sub-intervals with $y \ge y_0$ contribute $\sum_{y=y_0}^r (y - L_{\text{rich}}[y] + 1)$.
2. **Type 2 ($O((N + Q) \log^2 N)$ Offline Sweep)**:
   - Sort Type 2 queries by right endpoint $r$. Maintain an Euler-tour Segment Tree `SegMax` over the PAM `fail` tree (updating $\operatorname{dfn}[\operatorname{last}[r]] \leftarrow r$) so $\operatorname{prev\_r}(u) = \operatorname{SegMax.query}(\operatorname{dfn}[u], \operatorname{out}[u])$.
   - For $C(l, r)$, each `slink` chain performs 2 Fenwick point updates (`-1` at $\operatorname{prev\_r}(u_1) - \operatorname{len}[u_1] + 1$ and `+1` at $r - \operatorname{len}[u_k] + 1$).
   - For $\Sigma_{\text{len}}(l, r)$, run LCT `access(last[r])` on the PAM `fail` tree (where each splay node stores its static weight $\operatorname{len}[u]$ and subtree sum) or apply the `slink` AP difference updates.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-IV-05"}

- **Target Chapter & Technique ID**: **[Chapter 17](../chapters/ch17-range-palindromes-rich-words.qmd) (`T-3A-04` & `T-3A-05`: Factor-Closed Rich Word Threshold $L_{\text{rich}}[y]$ & Periodic Suffix Telescoping / LCT `access`; Decoy Pair B · Part 2)**.
- **Why Intermediate Nodes Cancel for $w(u) = 1$ But Leave $+d$ for $w(u) = \operatorname{len}[u]$**:
  Along a `slink` chain $u_1 \to u_2 \to \dots \to u_k$ of step $d = \operatorname{diff}[u_1]$ at step $r$, every non-head node $u_j$ ($2 \le j \le k$) is a proper palindromic border of $u_1$ of length $\ge |u_1| - d$ (for $j=2$), so its previous occurrence in $S[1..r-1]$ was the prefix copy inside $u_1$, ending at **$r - d$**.
  Consequently, $\operatorname{start}_{r-1}(u_j) = (r - d) - \operatorname{len}[u_j] + 1 = r - (\operatorname{len}[u_j] + d) + 1 = r - \operatorname{len}[u_{j-1}] + 1 = \operatorname{start}_r(u_{j-1})$.
  At start position $x = \operatorname{start}_r(u_{j-1})$, node $u_j$ departs with weight $-w(u_j)$ and node $u_{j-1}$ arrives with weight $+w(u_{j-1})$, producing net change $\Delta w = w(u_{j-1}) - w(u_j)$. When $w(u) = 1$, $\Delta w = 0$ (complete cancellation!); when $w(u) = \operatorname{len}[u]$, $\Delta w = \operatorname{len}[u_{j-1}] - \operatorname{len}[u_j] = +d$.

- **Boundary Pitfall Audit (`BP-4-07`, `BP-4-08`)**:
  - **Missing Factor Closure on Rich Substrings (`BP-4-07`)**: Never use 2D range structures to test or count Rich Substrings—the $O(N)$ Queue PAM two-pointer sweep computes $L_{\text{rich}}[1..N]$ in linear time and answers Type 1 in $O(\log N)$ (or $O(1)$ with an inverse lookup table).
  - **Scalar `last_end[u]` Instead of Subtree Maximum $\operatorname{prev\_r}(u_1)$ (`BP-4-08`)**: In `slink` telescoping, when $u_1$ is the head of a chain at step $r$, $u_1$ may have occurred more recently than its last visit as a chain head—specifically, whenever any descendant $w$ of $u_1$ in the PAM `fail` tree was visited! You **must** query $\operatorname{prev\_r}(u_1) = \operatorname{SegMax.query}(\operatorname{dfn}[u_1], \operatorname{out}[u_1])$ on the Euler tour of the PAM `fail` tree.
- **Complexity**: $O(N)$ for Type 1 preprocessing ($O(\log N)$ or $O(1)$ per query); $O((N + Q) \log^2 N)$ for Type 2.
::::

### Problem `CP-IV-06` — Run-Length Compressed Palindromic Spectrum & Substring 2-Palindrome Cuts

This problem has two parts testing compressed and factorized palindromic structure:

- **Part A (RLE Palindrome Spectrum)**: A massive string $S$ of total length $|S| \le 10^{14}$ is given in **Run-Length Encoded (RLE)** form as $M$ maximal contiguous runs $(c_1, k_1), (c_2, k_2), \dots, (c_M, k_M)$ ($1 \le M \le 10^5$, $c_i \ne c_{i+1}$, $1 \le k_i \le 10^9$). Compute:
  1. The total number of non-empty palindromic substrings of $S$ (with multiplicity) modulo $10^9 + 7$, and
  2. The exact number of **distinct** non-empty palindromic substrings of $S$.
- **Part B (Substring 2-Palindrome Cut Test)**: On an uncompressed string $T[1..N]$ ($N, Q \le 10^5$), given online queries $[l, r]$ ($r - l + 1 \ge 2$), decide in $O(\log(r - l))$ time whether $T[l..r] = P_1 P_2$ for two non-empty palindromes $P_1, P_2$.

- **Constraints**: $M, N, Q \le 10^5$, $k_i \le 10^9$, Time Limit $2.0\text{ s}$, Memory Limit $256\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}

- **Diagnostic Signal for Part A**: Since $|S| \le 10^{14}$, character-by-character Manacher or PAM is impossible. Ask: *Where can the center of a palindrome in $S$ lie relative to the run boundaries?*
  Because adjacent runs have distinct characters ($c_i \ne c_{i+1}$), a palindrome spanning $\ge 2$ runs can **never** be centered at the boundary between run $i$ and run $i+1$! Every palindrome in $S$ either:

  1. Lies **entirely inside a single run** $(c_i, k_i)$, OR
  2. Spans $2r + 1 \ge 3$ runs centered at the **exact midpoint of a full middle run** $(c_i, k_i)$!
- **Diagnostic Signal for Part B**: Why does testing *only* the single longest palindromic prefix $Q_1$ of $T[l..r]$ and single longest palindromic suffix $Q_2$ of $T[l..r]$ fail on $T[l..r] = \texttt{bababcba}$?
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}

1. **RLE Pair-Manacher & Outer-Wing Clamping Invariant (`W3A-38`)**:
   Treat the $M$ runs as a sequence of pairs $R_i = (c_i, k_i)$. A multi-run palindrome centered at run $i$ matches internal runs $1 \le j < r$ in **both character and exact run length**:
   $$(c_{i-j},\, k_{i-j}) = (c_{i+j},\, k_{i+j}) \qquad (\forall\, 1 \le j < r),$$
   while at the outer boundary $j = r$ (where $(c_{i-r}, k_{i-r}) \ne (c_{i+r}, k_{i+r})$), if $c_{i-r} = c_{i+r}$, the palindrome can still extend into both outer runs by $1, 2, \dots, \min(k_{i-r}, k_{i+r})$ characters!

   - **Multiplicity**: Run odd-center Manacher on the pair sequence $R[1..M]$! Each run $i$ contributes $\binom{k_i + 1}{2}$ intra-run palindromes, plus $\sum_{j=1}^{\text{rad}[i]-1} k_{i+j}$ for fully matched side runs, plus $\min(k_{i-\text{rad}[i]}, k_{i+\text{rad}[i]})$ if $c_{i-\text{rad}[i]} = c_{i+\text{rad}[i]}$.
   - **Distinct Count**: Single-run palindromes of character $c$ contribute $\max_{c_i = c} k_i$. Multi-run palindromes correspond to nodes $u$ of an **odd-length PAM built on the pair sequence $R[1..M]$**: each occurrence of node $u$ centered at $i$ (spanning runs $[i-r+1 .. i+r-1]$) that has $c_{i-r} = c_{i+r} = c$ generates $\min(k_{i-r}, k_{i+r})$ outer extensions of character $c$. Taking $\max_{\text{occ of } u} \min(k_{i-r}, k_{i+r})$ for each $(u, c)$ counts all distinct multi-run palindromes without duplicates!
2. **One-Sided Top-2-of-Each-AP Sufficiency for 2-Palindromes (`Ch 17` §4.2 / `T-3A-05`)**:
   On $T[l..r] = \texttt{bababcba} = \texttt{bab} + \texttt{abcba}$, the longest palindromic prefix is $Q_1 = \texttt{babab}$ (leaving $\texttt{cba}$, not a palindrome!), while the valid prefix $P_1 = \texttt{bab} = \operatorname{fail}[Q_1]$ is the **second** node in $Q_1$'s `slink` arithmetic progression!
   By `Ch 17` §4.2, if $T[l..r] = P_1 P_2$, then either $P_1$ is one of the **top 2 nodes** ($u$ or $\operatorname{fail}[u]$) of one of the $O(\log(r-l))$ `slink` chains of $P_L(l, r)$, OR $P_2$ is one of the **top 2 nodes** of one of the $O(\log(r-l))$ `slink` chains of $P_R(l, r)$!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}

1. **Part A Assembly ($O(M \log M)$)**:
   - Run odd Manacher on $R_i = (c_i, k_i)$ to sum multiplicity in $O(M)$ time.
   - Build an odd-root-only PAM on $R_1, \dots, R_M$ (or use the Suffix Array / `height` Cartesian tree of $R[1..M]$ centered at odd Manacher intervals) to group identical core run-palindromes $u$ and accumulate $\max \min(k_{i-r}, k_{i+r})$ per outer character $c$.
2. **Part B Assembly ($O(\log(r - l))$ per query)**:
   - Use `CP-IV-02`'s `slink` ceiling division on $\operatorname{PAM}(T^R)$ from $\operatorname{first}[l]$ (capped at length $r - l$) to visit the $O(\log(r-l))$ `slink` chain heads of palindromic prefixes of $T[l..r]$.
   - At each chain head $u$, test both $|P_1| = \operatorname{len}[u]$ and (if $\operatorname{len}[u] - \operatorname{diff}[u] > \operatorname{len}[\operatorname{slink}[u]]$) $|P_1| = \operatorname{len}[u] - \operatorname{diff}[u]$ by checking in $O(1)$ via Manacher whether the remaining suffix $T[l + |P_1| .. r]$ is a palindrome! Repeat symmetrically from $\operatorname{last}[r]$ on $\operatorname{PAM}(T)$.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-IV-06"}

- **Target Chapter & Technique ID**: **[Chapter 17](../chapters/ch17-range-palindromes-rich-words.qmd) (`T-3A-05`: RLE Pair-Manacher/PAM Compression & Top-2-of-Each-AP 2-Palindrome Sufficiency Theorem; `[AtCoder AGC / JOI]` `W3A-38` & `W3A-40`)**.
- **Why Testing the Top 2 Nodes per `slink` AP Chain Suffices for 2-Palindromes**:
  Suppose $T[l..r] = P_1 P_2$ where $P_1$ belongs to a `slink` chain of the longest palindromic prefix $Q_1$ with period $d = \operatorname{diff}[Q_1]$, and suppose $P_1$ is neither the chain head $u_1$ nor the second node $u_2 = u_1 - d$ (so $|u_1| \ge |P_1| + 2d$).
  Because $u_1$ is a palindromic prefix of $T[l..r]$ of period $d$ extending at least $2d$ past $P_1$, the prefix of $P_2$ of length $|u_1| - |P_1| \ge 2d$ has period $d$. Specifically, $u_1 = P_1 M$ being a palindrome with $|M| < |P_2|$ forces $M^R$ to be a prefix of $P_1$, and whenever $|M| \ge 2d$, periodicity alignment across the cut point guarantees that either $u_1$ or $u_2 = u_1 - d$ leaves a valid palindrome!

- **Boundary Pitfall Audit (`BP-4-07`)**:
  - **Testing Only the Single Longest Palindromic Prefix/Suffix (`BP-4-07`)**: Fails on $W = \texttt{bababcba} = \texttt{bab} + \texttt{abcba}$, where the longest palindromic prefix $Q_1 = \texttt{babab}$ over-extends by one period step $d = 2$ and leaves $\texttt{cba}$ (non-palindrome). Always test both $u$ and $\operatorname{fail}[u]$ in each `slink` chain.
- **Complexity**: $O(M \log M)$ for Part A; $O(N)$ preprocessing and $O(\log(r - l))$ per query for Part B.
::::

### Problem `CP-IV-07` — Single-Point Mutation Palindrome Healing

You are given a string $S[1..N]$ of lowercase letters ($1 \le N \le 2 \times 10^5$) and $Q$ independent what-if queries ($1 \le Q \le 2 \times 10^5$). Each query specifies a position $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ and a replacement lowercase character $c \in \{\texttt{'a'}, \dots, \texttt{'z'}\}$, and asks:

> If we temporarily change $S[i]$ to $c$ (leaving all other characters of $S$ unchanged), what is the **total number of non-empty palindromic substrings (counted with multiplicity)** in the modified string?

- **Constraints**: $1 \le N, Q \le 2 \times 10^5$, $|\Sigma| = 26$, Time Limit $1.5\text{ s}$, Memory Limit $256\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}

- **Decoy Elimination**: Re-running Manacher per query takes $\Theta(QN)$. Moreover, a single character mutation at index $i$ affects palindromes centered across the entire string $S[1..N]$, so neither a local window nor a PAM fail-tree walk applies directly.
- **Diagnostic Signal (`Ch 17` Manacher Geometry + `Ch 15` $O(1)$ LCE Synthesis)**:
  Let $T_0 = \sum_{m} d[m]$ be the baseline total number of palindromes in $S$. When $S[i]$ is changed to $c \ne S[i]$, decompose the net change $\Delta(i, c)$ across all $2N - 1$ Manacher centers $m$ into two independent effects:

  1. **Destruction (`destroyed[i]`, independent of $c \ne S[i]$!)**: Any center $m \ne i$ whose baseline Manacher palindrome strictly covers index $i$ now mismatches at $i$ and its mirror $2m - i$, losing all outer radii from $|m - i|$ up to its baseline radius!
  2. **Creation / Mismatch Healing (`healed[i][c]`)**: Which centers $m$ can **gain** new palindromic radii when $S[i]$ becomes $c$? **Only** those centers $m$ whose **very first mismatch** in the baseline string $S$ landed at index $i$ (and whose opposite boundary character equals $c$)!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}

1. **Second-Order Difference Array for Destruction Pyramids (`destroyed[1..N]`)**:
   Consider an odd center $m \in [1, N]$ with baseline odd radius $d_1[m] \ge 2$ (spanning $[m - d_1[m] + 1, \; m + d_1[m] - 1]$).

   - Changing $S[m]$ itself **never** destroys any odd palindrome centered at $m$!
   - For any $i \in [m - d_1[m] + 1, \; m - 1]$ (and symmetrically $i \in [m + 1, \; m + d_1[m] - 1]$), changing $S[i]$ to any $c \ne S[i]$ truncates center $m$'s radius from $d_1[m]$ down to $m - i$, destroying exactly:
     $$\Delta_{\text{loss}}(m, i) = d_1[m] - |m - i| \quad \text{palindromes!}$$
   Notice that $i \mapsto d_1[m] - |m - i|$ is a **linear progression of slope $+1$** on $[m - d_1[m] + 1, m - 1]$ and **slope $-1$** on $[m + 1, m + d_1[m] - 1]$! The exact same linear ramp holds for even centers $d_2[m]$. Thus we can accumulate `destroyed[1..N]` across all $2N - 1$ centers simultaneously in **$O(N)$ total time** using a **2nd-order difference array (prefix sums of prefix sums)**!

2. **Mismatch Healing via `Ch 15` $O(1)$ LCE (`healed[i][c]`)**:
   For each center $m$, let its first mismatch outside its baseline Manacher interval be the pair of indices $(l_m, r_m) = (m - d_1[m], \; m + d_1[m])$ (if $1 \le l_m$ and $r_m \le N$).
   If we change $S[l_m]$ to $c = S[r_m]$ (or change $S[r_m]$ to $c = S[l_m]$), the mismatch at $(l_m, r_m)$ is **healed**, and center $m$'s radius expands by:
   $$\Delta_{\text{gain}}(m) = 1 + \operatorname{LCE}_{S, S^R}\bigl(l_m - 1,\; r_m + 1\bigr)!$$
   Since there are only $2N - 1$ centers $m$, there are **at most $2(2N - 1)$ healing events** $(l_m, S[r_m])$ and $(r_m, S[l_m])$ across the entire string!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}

1. Run Manacher's algorithm on $S[1..N]$ to obtain $d_1[1..N]$, $d_2[1..N-1]$, and baseline total $T_0 = \sum d_1[m] + \sum d_2[m]$.
2. Build the Suffix Array + $O(1)$ RMQ on $S \# S^R$ (or $S$ and $S^R$) in $O(N \log N)$ time to support $O(1)$ outward $\operatorname{LCE}_{S, S^R}(x, y) = \operatorname{LCP}(S[1..x]^R, S[y..N])$.
3. For each of the $2N - 1$ centers $m$:
   - Add its two linear destruction ramps on $[m - d + 1, m - 1]$ and $[m + 1, m + d - 1]$ to a 2nd-order difference array `diff2[1..N+2]`.
   - If its first mismatch pair $(l_m, r_m)$ lies inside $[1, N]^2$, compute $g = 1 + \operatorname{LCE}_{S, S^R}(l_m - 1, r_m + 1)$ in $O(1)$ time, and add $+g$ to both `healed[l_m][S[r_m] - 'a']` and `healed[r_m][S[l_m] - 'a']`.
4. Integrate `diff2` twice to obtain `destroyed[1..N]`.
5. Answer each query $(i, c)$ in **$O(1)$ time**: if $c == S[i]$, output $T_0$; else output $T_0 - \text{destroyed}[i] + \text{healed}[i][c - \texttt{'a'}]$.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-IV-07"}

- **Target Chapter & Technique ID**: **[Chapter 15](../chapters/ch15-internal-pattern-matching-borders.qmd) & [Chapter 17](../chapters/ch17-range-palindromes-rich-words.qmd) (`T-2B-04` + `T-3A-03`: Basic Substring Dictionary $O(1)$ LCE Mismatch Healing & Manacher 2nd-Order Difference Pyramids, `[ICPC Regional / UCup]` `W3A-39`)**.
- **Why Only the First Mismatch Boundary $(l_m, r_m)$ Can Be Healed**:
  A single-point query mutates **at most one character** $S[i] \leftarrow c$. For any center $m$ where $i$ lies outside its baseline Manacher palindrome ($i \le l_m$ or $i \ge r_m$), if $i < l_m$ or $i > r_m$, the mismatch at $(l_m, r_m)$ remains untouched and still blocks any expansion of center $m$ past $(l_m, r_m)$! Thus center $m$ can expand past its baseline radius **if and only if** the mutated position $i$ is one of the two endpoints $l_m$ or $r_m$ of its first mismatch, and the new character $c$ equals the opposite endpoint!

- **Boundary Pitfall Audit (`BP-4-05`)**:
  - **Subtracting `destroyed` at the Center $i = m$ Itself & Parity Separation (`BP-4-05`)**: For an odd palindrome centered at $m$, index $m$ is its own mirror ($2m - m = m$). Replacing $S[m]$ with any character $c$ leaves $S[m] = S[m]$ trivially satisfied, so **zero** odd palindromes centered at $m$ are destroyed when $S[m]$ changes! Always stop the left ramp at $m - 1$ and start the right ramp at $m + 1$, and handle odd centers $d_1[m]$ and even centers $d_2[m]$ with their separate mirror coordinates ($2m - i$ vs. $2m + 1 - i$).
- **Complexity**: $O(N \log N)$ (or $O(N)$ with SA-IS) preprocessing and **strict $O(1)$ time per query**, in $O(N |\Sigma|)$ space.
::::

Query open interval $[c_L+1, c_R-1]$. |

Always query the fail-tree subtree max. |

::::
